# The optimizers7 package {#sec-optimizers7}

The last chapter ended with a maximisation performed by three fixed routines,
and with the admission that the user could not supply a fourth. This chapter is
about removing that limitation, and about what has to be true of an optimisation
routine before it is safe to let anyone plug one in.

The mathematics divides cleanly, and none of it is new: @nocedal2006 is the
standard modern account of almost everything in this chapter, with @dennis1983
and @bonnans2006 as the other two books a reader might keep to hand. What
follows states the results the implementations rest on and says where each comes
from, rather than reproving them. @sec-descent asks what it means to take a step
at all: what makes a direction a descent direction, what a line search along it
must guarantee, and why a condition on the objective alone is not enough — the
result there, Zoutendijk's, is the one that turns "each step decreases $f$" into
"the gradient goes to zero", which is a very different claim. @sec-curvature
then asks how to choose the direction, and takes the methods in order of how
much they store. Newton's uses the exact Hessian and must repair it when it is
not positive definite; the quasi-Newton methods refuse to compute one and build
an approximation from the gradients they have already seen, which turns out to
be determined almost uniquely by two requirements; and below them are methods
keeping a few pairs of vectors, then one vector, then a single number. What is
worth noticing on the way down is how far one can go before the method stops
working, and that the answer is very nearly all the way.

@sec-nonsmooth is where the picture changes. Everything before it assumes a
gradient that becomes small near a solution, and for an objective with a kink in
it — a sum of absolute deviations, a Laplace likelihood in its location — that
assumption is simply false: the subgradient at the minimiser has norm one. A
method built on it does not merely converge slowly, it arrives at the answer and
then reports failure. Two repairs are possible, and both are here: abandon
derivatives entirely, which costs a great deal and buys a weaker theorem, or
keep them and stop asking any single one of them to vanish, which is the bundle
method. @neldermead1965 belongs to the first camp and @lemarechal1975 to the
second.

@sec-constraints turns to two things that sit outside the descent framework
rather than inside it. Box constraints are removed by a change of variable, so
that no algorithm ever learns a constraint was involved; and Adam takes steps
that are not descent steps at all, which is the price of tolerating a gradient
computed from a handful of observations.

@sec-starting closes with the question every run has to answer before it can
begin, which is where to start. The natural answer is wrong in a way worth
seeing, and the right one turns out to be the change of variable of the section
before it; and asking it properly leads to a second question no single run can
address, namely how many answers the problem has.
